Title: Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Fragment of a clay tablet: containing epigraphs for a series of carved wall panels. The text is written in twenty-eight lines of cuneiform script. Upper half, part of a text containing epigraphs with relate to Assurbanipal's campaigns; they probably forme;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: across the face Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: This text gives a list of captions for the series of carved wall-panels. It is one of several such lists, and a few of the captions on the texts correspond closely to those on surviving panels. The theme may have been represented several times over in different rooms. It is unclear whether the tablets were written in the course of designing the series or as a record of captions already on the walls.;

(17) [la i-m]a-gùr-ru Inscription translation: To HM the King!
Your servant Nabuasharid:
May Ashur and Esharra bless the King!
Re the matter the King has asked me: (PN₁) and Bēl-ibni . . . (ll. 8-10 too fragmentary for translation). We have now sent two royal statues to the King. I have made the one which has ‘form’; the made the one which is of a certain clumsiness. May the King have a look! We shall finish the one that the King prefers. The King should pay special attention to the hands, the chin and the hairdo. On the statue which they are making the sceptre is placed across his arm and his arm rests on his hip. I do not agree with this and shall not make it. If I talk to them on good taste or anything else, they do not even listen. They . . . on their own . . . (ll. 13-15 too fragmentary for translation). I want to do . . . but they do not agree. Inscription note: There are 23 lines of inscription on this fragment. The transliteration and translation are for the whole letter. Title: Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Fragment of a clay tablet, omens, 22 + 11 lines of inscription, Neo-Assyrian. Upper portion, left half. A manuscript of chapter 4 of the treatise addressing conditions affecting the cranium, as part of the Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: (o i 1–o i 2) If a man’s head is full of sweet lesions due to sunburn: you mix pulp from irrû-plant (‘cucumber’), stone from irrû-plant (and) . . . in oil from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’), (and) you keep anointing his head (with the mixture).
(o i 3–o i 4) If DITTO, you dry (and) pound the plant(?), which(?) is like(?) ēru-tree (and) murrānu (‘myrrh-like’ plant) is its name, you anoint his head three times with it in oil from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’), (and then) he should smear off (the anointment) with a cloth of date palm fiber, (which) he should burn once he cleaned himself.
(o i 5–o i 6) If DITTO, you dry (and) pound (a drug), its name is murru (‘myrrh’), you mix it in water, you keep anoint his head with it, (and then) he should smear off (the anointment) with a cloth of date palm fiber, (which) he should burn once he cleaned himself. You mix imḫur-līm-plant (‘faces a thousand’ plant) in oil from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’), (and) you keep anointing him with it.
(o i 7–o i 11) If a man’s head is full of sweet lesions: you parch pig bristle, salt, isqūqu (a type of groats) (and) sheep bone, you shave his head, you anoint it with oil, (and) you scatter (the drugs over the anointment). You anoint (his head) with oil, you pound šammu peṣû (‘white plant’), (and) you scatter it (over the anointment). You dry, crush (and) scatter root from irrû-plant (‘cucumber’) (over his head). You parch, pound flour from buqlu (‘malt’), isqūqu (a type of groats) (and) sheep bone together, (and) you scatter them (over his head). You bring to a boils annuḫaru-mineral (and) gabû-stone (‘alum’) over and over again, you pound them together, you keep anointing (his head) with them in oil, (and) you scatter(?) (the drugs over the anointment). You roast . . . (and) you scatter it (over his head). You anoint (his head) with vinegar, you pound nīnû-plant (‘mint’), (and) you scatter it (over the anointment). You knead river mud in juice from suluppū (‘dates’), (and) you bandage him (with the mixture). You roast kalbānu-plant, you anoint (his head) with ghee, (and) you bandage him with it. You pound . . . (and) you scatter it (over his head). You pound nurmû-tree (‘pomegranate’), (and) you scatter it (over his head). You knead sheep dung in beer, (and) you bandage him (with the mixture). You parch (and) pound . . . (and) you bandage him with it.
(o i 12–o i 13) If a man’s head is full of sweet lesions: you shave his head, you pound saḫlû (‘cress’), you put it all together in ten shekels of resin from baluḫḫu-aromatic (‘galbanum’), five shekels of ṭūru-aromatic (‘opopanax’), ten shekels of uḫūlu qarnānû (‘horned alkali’), kukru-aromatic (and) burāšu-aromatic (‘juniper’), you mix them in vinegar, you bandage him (with the mixture) for five days, and then he will recover.
(o i 14–o i 15) If DITTO, you burn amānu-salt, you combine copper patina(?) (and) gabû-stone (‘alum’) together, you mix them (all) in vinegar, you bandage him (with the mixture), and then you do not remove (the bandage) for three days. While you are removing it, you wash him with warm urine, you anoint him with flour(?) from bappiru(?)-bread (and) blood from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’), you scatter these drugs (over the anointment) for five days, you bandage him with them, and then he will recover.
(o i 16–o i 17) If DITTO, you pound rušruššu-plant, šammu peṣû (‘white plant’), peel from nurmû-tree (‘pomegranate’), stone from suluppū (‘dates’), kirbān eqli-plant (‘field lump’ plant), roasted(?) saḫlû(?) (‘cress’), fruit from nīnû-plant (‘mint’), nuḫurtu-plant (‘asafoetida’) (and) zibû (‘black cumin’) in a mortar, you keep anointing him with flour(?) from bappiru(?)-bread (and) blood from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’), you scatter these drugs (over the anointment), you bandage him with them, and then he will recover.
(o i 18–o i 19) If DITTO, you knead warm urine of an ox in strong vinegar, you bandage him for three days (with the mixture) . . . (and) you place it over the lesion. You parch (and) pound būšānu-plant (‘smelly’ plant) (and) stones from suluppū (‘dates’) . . . (and) you scatter them (over the lesion).
(o i 20–o i 21) If DITTO, . . . sour nurmûtree (‘pomegranate’), zibû (‘black cumin’) . . . dišpu (‘syrup’) . . . you heat them over fire . . . you wash (and) shave his head . . . you anoint(?) him, and then he will recover.
(o i 22–o i 23) If a man’s head is full of sweet lesions . . .
(r ii 1'–r ii 2') If(?) a man(?) . . . his(?) head(?) . . .
(r ii 3'–r ii 4') If DITTO, you crush (and) sift uḫūlu qarnānû (‘horned alkali’) . . . If DITTO, . . . his head with warm cow urine . . .
(r ii 5') If the middle of a man's heaad constantly causes him a stingin pain, you anoint his cranium . . .
(r ii 6') Fourth tablet of (the series called) “If a man’s cranium retains heat.”
(r ii 7') Palace of Aššur-ban-apli, king of the universe, king of the land of Aššur, on whom Nabû and Tašmētu have bestowed wisdom.
(r ii 8') He acquired for himself shining eyes, the pinnacle of scholarship.
(r ii 9') Of the kings who came before me, none were able to comprehend these tasks.
(r ii 10') Prescriptions (organised) from head to foot, gleanings from extraneous materials, technical lore
(r ii 11') (and) whatever pertains to the great medical knowledge of Ninurta and Gula, I have written on tablets, checked, collated, and
(r ii 12') deposited them in the middle of my palace for my reading and recitation.;

Title: Library of Ashurbanipal
Description: Fragment of a clay tablet, 8 lines of inscription, Neo-Assyrian. A manuscript of chapter 3 of the treatise addressing conditions affecting the cranium, as part of the Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia.;
Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: (r i 1'–r i 2') Incantation: “May the temple bring his temple back (to health), may the eye bring his eye back (to health), may the middle (of the head) bring his middle (of the head) back (to health). May he be able to shine, may he be able to shine.” Incantation-formula.
(r i 3'–r i 5') Its ritual: you twist male ašlu-plant (a rush) (and) gazelle sinew together (into a thread), you tie seven and seven knots on it, (and) with each knot you recite the incantation, you wrap male and female ḫallulāyu-insect (and) . . ., which flies over the field, around the knots in red wool, (and) you tie (the string) on his temple.
(r i 6'–r i 8')
(r ii 1'–r ii 3') If a man’s left ear is affected, it is full of wind (and) inflamed: on the fifteenth day of the sixth month, you heat up goose fat (and) while it is still steaming hot, you pour it into his ears. You heat up goose meat, (and) he eats it. You pour oil from erēnu-tree (‘cedar’) on his head, (and) he eats ḫibṣu-preparation in saḫlû (‘cress’).;
